title: Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors
audience: Timber floor restoration workers, and the supervisors who approve sanding and stripping work.
learningOutcomes: Explain why old paint, varnish, adhesive and vinyl can contain hazardous material that appearance does not rule out.
Apply a stop-and-refer decision when a floor may contain lead or asbestos.
Describe the kind of controls that a documented assessment must set before any disturbance.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government, LeadSmart: renovating and maintenance (published 18 May 2026; last modified 20 July 2026); Safe Work Australia, Lead: WHS duties and lead risk work (no date shown); SafeWork SA, Asbestos licences: Class A, Class B and assessor licence (no date shown).

instruction.heading: Why old finishes are a hazard
instruction.body: Timber floors in older buildings can carry layers of paint, varnish and adhesive from earlier work. NSW LeadSmart (page published 18 May 2026) says most Australian homes built before 1970 contained lead paint. Floor coverings and adhesives in older buildings may also contain asbestos. Neither lead nor asbestos can be ruled out by how a surface looks.

instruction.heading: Lead in old finishes
instruction.body: The main concern is lead dust produced by sanding or scraping. Safe Work Australia's lead page (no date shown) treats grinding and sanding that expose workers to lead dust as lead processes, and links lead risk work to a blood lead level above 5 µg/dL for a female of reproductive capacity or above 20 µg/dL in any other case. Treat the surface as possibly lead-containing until a documented assessment, using a method the assessor specifies, says otherwise.

instruction.heading: Asbestos in floor coverings and adhesive
instruction.body: Asbestos may be present in older vinyl, floor tiles, sheet flooring and adhesives. In South Australia, SafeWork SA's page (no date shown) says that friable asbestos and asbestos-backed vinyl need a Class A removal licence, and that non-friable material such as floor tiles falls under a Class B licence where more than 10 square metres is removed (the SafeWork SA applicant guide). A worker must not remove, grind or sand suspected asbestos material in order to find out what it is.

instruction.heading: The stop-and-refer decision
instruction.body: If the assessment cannot rule out lead or asbestos, stop work on that area, keep people out of it, record the finding, and refer it to the supervisor and to the approved assessor or licensed contractor. The error this lesson addresses is carrying on with sanding because the floor looks sound. Do not treat a finish as safe because an earlier contractor worked on it. Clear only the area that the assessment covers, and record that boundary.

instruction.heading: Controls once the material is known
instruction.body: Where an assessment finds lead or asbestos, the controls come from that assessment and from the regulator's requirements, not from this training. NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) describes wet sanding and wet scraping as the safest way to prepare a surface with lead paint, advises keeping pregnant or breastfeeding women and young children away from renovation work, and advises against open-flame torches. These are NSW government statements, not a national control plan.

procedure: Ask the client about the building age and any earlier work, and record the answer.
Look for layers of paint, varnish, adhesive, vinyl or tile in and near the floor area.
Do not sand, scrape, cut or grind a suspect area in order to test it.
If lead or asbestos cannot be ruled out, stop work on that area and keep people away from it.
Refer the finding to the supervisor and record it with photos and the location.
Do not restart the area until the written assessment and its required controls are in place.

workedExamples.situation: A client in a 1960s home asks you to sand the hallway floor. A thick painted border runs around the room, and black adhesive is visible at an edge where old vinyl was removed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct decision, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop before any sanding in the affected area. The painted border may contain lead, and the black adhesive may contain asbestos. Neither can be confirmed by sight. Keep people away from the area, record the finding with photos and location, and refer it to the supervisor for a documented assessment and any licensed removal. The rest of the floor is not cleared by this, and it must not be treated as safe by default.

equipmentAndPpe: Barrier tape or signage for the affected area
Approved respirator and PPE for the assessment visit, if the assessment plan requires it (see “Respiratory protection and fit: the last layer of control”)

commonErrors.error: Sanding the floor first and asking questions later.
commonErrors.prevention: Assess and stop before any machine is used.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a painted border or black adhesive is harmless.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat it as suspect until it has been assessed.

commonErrors.error: Scraping or cutting a sample to test it.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the written assessment method.

commonErrors.error: Continuing in the unaffected area as if the whole job is cleared.
commonErrors.prevention: Clear only the area the assessment covers, and record the boundary.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant authority to assess or remove lead or asbestos. Where the law requires a licence or a competent person, only that person may do the work.
Lead in old finishes: NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) says most Australian homes built before 1970 contained lead paint.
Asbestos: SafeWork SA (page date not shown) sets out Class A and Class B removal licences and an assessor licence.
Refer any sanding of lead-painted timber before work starts.

qualityStandard: Suspect areas are identified and marked before any machine is used.
No suspect material is disturbed without a written assessment and its controls.
Every stop and referral is recorded with location, photos and the person informed.
documentationEvidence: Pre-start hazard assessment with a finding for each area
Stop-work record and referral, with the date and the person informed
Assessment report and controls, where obtained
summary: Old paint, varnish, adhesive and vinyl may contain hazardous material.
If lead or asbestos cannot be ruled out, stop, keep people away and refer.
Do not disturb suspect material to test it.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: NSW Government, LeadSmart: renovating and maintenance (published 18 May 2026; last modified 20 July 2026); Safe Work Australia, Lead: WHS duties and lead risk work (no date shown); SafeWork SA, Asbestos licences: Class A, Class B and assessor licence (no date shown).

knowledgeChecks.question: A floor edge has black adhesive and a thick painted border. What do you do?
options: Sand the adhesive off quickly with a belt sander
Cut a sample of the paint and test it for lead
Stop work on that area and refer it for assessment
Continue because it looks old and quite worn

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must old paint not be treated as safe by sight?
options: Paint always contains asbestos in older houses
Old paint is always safe to disturb and sand
Only metal surfaces can carry lead paint at all
Lead cannot be confirmed by appearance alone

knowledgeChecks.question: In South Australia, which licence covers removal of non-friable asbestos such as floor tiles?
options: A Class B licence
An assessor licence
A Class C licence
No licence needed

knowledgeChecks.question: Which action does NSW LeadSmart recommend when preparing old paint?
options: Dry sanding with a vacuum
Wet sanding or wet scraping
Open-flame stripping of paint
Sanding in a closed room

knowledgeChecks.question: The client says the floor is fine because a previous builder checked it. What is correct?
options: Accept the claim and start sanding the floor today
Remove the adhesive with a scraper straight away
Record the claim, but still assess before any disturbance
Stop the job and leave the area open to the public
